page: Microsoft Azure M96bs_v3 is a memory-optimized virtual machine driven by the x86_64 Intel Xeon 8473C processor operating at frequencies up to 4.0 GHz. Built on Microsoft Hyper-V, the system provides 96 dedicated vCPUs distributed over 48 physical cores with two threads per core. System memory totals 768.0 GB of RAM, establishing an 8.0 GB per vCPU allocation ratio. The hardware architecture features a 105 MB L3 cache alongside support for hardware-accelerated instruction sets including Intel AMX (tile and int8) and AVX-512. The instance contains no integrated local storage and features zero GPUs, utilizing remote block storage for operating system and data requirements.

Benchmark evaluations indicate upper-tier multi-threaded processing power and high memory throughput. The server delivered a PassMark CPU score of 97408.44 and a stress-ng multi-core measurement of 91332.66, complemented by top-tier results in extended instruction testing at 121966.92. Memory bandwidth reaches 428.2 GB/sec for large uncached reads and 184.37 GB/sec for large write operations. In workload-specific benchmarks, the system handled 34584.01 PassMark database operations, 114.5 million Redis SET operations per second, and 112.86 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. Single-core performance remains balanced, recording 2057.09 in stress-ng and 2209.0 in Geekbench.

The primary tradeoff of the M96bs_v3 configuration lies in its storage architecture. Without local NVMe drives, storage throughput and latency depend entirely on external attached block volumes. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the high memory-to-core density allows organizations running massive in-memory datasets to consolidate workloads onto fewer large nodes instead of over-provisioning compute resources across smaller general-purpose instances.

The M96bs_v3 is structured specifically for memory-intensive enterprise environments. Its primary workload fits include large in-memory caching layers such as Redis, enterprise database engines, in-memory analytics platforms, high-throughput static web frontends, and CPU-driven batch processing jobs leveraging AMX matrix acceleration.
